To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified a new mechanism for eliciting tier 2 neutralization, which may inform vaccine design.

native, membrane-exposed, glycosylated HIV-1 Env trimers are able to elicit neutralizing antibodies in rabbits, that the elicited antibodies target quaternary epitope, and that they can exploit holes in the glycosylation shield that mask the CD4 binding region.
we have shown for the first time, using rabbit sera, that strain-specific holes or gaps in the glycosylation of HIV-1 Env can elicit potent neutralizing antibodies to the native spike.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an effective HIV vaccine.
the ability of native HIV-1 Envelope glycoprotein trimer to elicit neutralizing antibodies (Abs).
the development of a neutralization antibody vaccine against HIV-1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

1) the N197 and N230 glycan-deficient regions of the HIV-1 Env trimer, which are proximal to the conserved CD4 binding site (CD4bs) and the V2 region, can elicit neutralizing antibodies in rabbits; and 2) neutralizing antibodies elicited by the N197-deficient Env trimer exploit the natural absence of this N197 glycan to target the CD4bs.
we have shown for the first time, that holes in the glycoprotein spikes of the HIV virus can allow for development of neutralizing antibodies.
we have identified two new epitopes that can be targeted by neutralizing antibodies, and that these antibodies can develop in response to immunization with native Env trimers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the glycan fence is not an insurmountable barrier for elicitation of potent neutralizing antibodies.
we have shown for the first time the ability of native trimers to elict broad neutralizing antibodies.
we have shown that native, unclipped, trimer spikes can be used as immunogens to elicit tier 2 neutralization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of tier two neutralizing antibodies to the native spike can occur in the presence of holes in the glycosylation shield of HIV-1.

the absence of glycan at residue N197 in gp120 of the JR-FL isolate can lead to the elicitation of neutralizing antibodies that are able to neutralize a significant proportion of clade B isolates that do not have this glycan.
holes in the glycosylation of HIV-1 envelope trimers, which are not rare, can allow the development and cross-reactivity of tier 2 antibodies.
